question: How does the parameter count for prefix-layer tuning compare to that of prefix-embedding tuning, and what structural difference causes this difference?
context: We use lp (resp. li) denote the number of preﬁx (resp. inﬁx) tokens. The number of trainable parameters is |Θ| = dmodel × (lp + li). Preﬁx-layer tuning (PreLayer) is an extension to preﬁx-embedding tuning. Instead of just learning the word embeddings (or equivalently, the activations after the embedding layer) for some special tokens, we learn the activations after every Transformer layer. The activations computed from previous layers are simply replaced by trainable ones. The resulting number of trainable parameters is |Θ| = L × dmodel × (lp + li), where L is the number of Transformer layers.
gold_answer: Prefix-layer tuning has L times more trainable parameters than prefix-embedding tuning because it learns trainable activations after every Transformer layer (L layers), whereas prefix-embedding tuning only learns embeddings once (i.e., after the embedding layer).

  chunked_output = jnp.vectorize(multi_neighbour_cross_attention,

question: Why does Verify-and-Edit incur lower computational costs than ReAct, according to the text?
context: As cost reduction is a main concern when interacting with LLMs, our method takes it into consideration and attempts to reduce computational costs from two aspects: Firstly, Verify-and-Edit only makes edits for selected instances, whereas others edit every time. Speciﬁcally, we only revise when the model is uncertain (judged by consistency), which occurs 40% of the time. As a comparison, other methods, such as ReAct, retrieve relevant information and edit for every single instance, resulting in higher costs. Secondly, Verify-and-Edit designs tasks that are natural and conversational, requiring only a few demonstrations and short prompts to learn. For example, other methods usually learn non-natural calls, such as [thought] and [action] tags in ReAct and API calls in Toolformer (Schick et al., 2023). Therefore, the LLM requires longer prompts, more demonstrations, or even ﬁne-tuning to learn the format.
